title: Tenali Raman and the Golden Mango Saplings

full_text:
A wealthy and selfish courtier named Ramabhadra discovered that King Krishnadevaraya had imported fifty rare, graft-bred mango saplings capable of bearing sweet golden fruit twice a year.
Using his influence with the royal chief gardener, Ramabhadra bribed the staff, diverted all fifty saplings to his own private country estate, and left none for the public orchards!
When citizens inquired about the promised distribution, the corrupt gardener claimed: 'Alas! A blight of locusts ate all the saplings in the nursery!'

Tenali Raman suspected foul play.
He visited Ramabhadra’s estate disguised as a traveling soil chemist from Ujjain.
Walking through the private walled orchard, Tenali saw the fifty rare saplings planted in neat, irrigated rows, thriving with green shoots.

Tenali returned to the palace and whispered to King Krishnadevaraya:
'Maharaj, a rare and miraculous golden herb grows in Ramabhadra's orchard! Its leaves possess the supernatural power to double the yield of all fruit trees in the kingdom, but only if they are transplanted into the communal fields within three days!'

The King, accompanied by his ministers and Tenali, rode unannounced to Ramabhadra’s estate.
When the gates opened, the King was shocked to see all fifty of his imported royal mango saplings growing in Ramabhadra's private soil!
The King’s brow darkened with thunder:
'Ramabhadra! The chief gardener told me these saplings were eaten by locusts! Art thou the two-legged locust who ate the royal nursery?'

Ramabhadra fell to his knees in terror, begging for mercy.
Tenali smiled and said:
'Maharaj, let the punishment fit the crime!
Ramabhadra loved these saplings so dearly that he must be granted the honor of planting them!
Order Ramabhadra to dig up all fifty saplings with his own hands, carry them on his own shoulders to the public gardens of the weavers' quarter, replant them in the communal soil, and water them every dawn for one full year!'

The King approved the verdict with a hearty laugh.
The proud, wealthy courtier was stripped of his fine silks, handed a spade, and spent the entire year digging holes and carrying water buckets for the poor weavers.
The mango saplings flourished, yielding sweet fruit for hundreds of children, proving that public blessings belong to the community, not to the greed of a few.
moral: Greed that tries to corner agricultural blessings is cured when made to tend the soil of the poor.
